author: John Chrysostom
occasion: A festal homily delivered on the day after Epiphany, when the feast of Christ's baptism had ended and many of the congregation had departed. Chrysostom continues his previous exhortation to those who remain and honors the martyr Lucian, whose martyrdom he presents as a baptism in blood on this day.
argument: Chrysostom laments that after yesterday's feast the crowd has departed, and he urges those present to value the church as a spiritual ark that protects against worldly passions and the instability of wealth. He then turns to the martyr Lucian, describing how the devil first tried to break him by prolonged hunger, and when that failed, added the further trial of placing idol-food before his eyes. Lucian endured both, sustained by hope, the example of Paul, and the fear of God. At his trial Lucian answered every question only with 'I am a Christian,' showing that this one confession contains his homeland, citizenship, family, and occupation. Chrysostom concludes by exhorting the congregation to train in peace for the contests of war, to confess the faith boldly, and to adorn that confession with a worthy life.

outline.move: Chrysostom laments the smaller crowd after yesterday's feast and praises the church as a spiritual ark that protects against passions and the instability of wealth.

He contrasts the blessings of attending church with the loss suffered by those who have departed, and introduces the martyr's contest by comparing yesterday's baptism of Christ in water with today's baptism of the servant in blood.
He describes the devil's scheme to break Lucian first by hunger and then by displaying idol-food before him, and how Lucian's endurance and fear of God overcame both nature and the bait.

The table of the three youths in Babylon is brought to Lucian's mind, and he is brought to trial, where he answers every question only with 'I am a Christian,' a reply that contains his whole identity.
Chrysostom exhorts the congregation to imitate Lucian by confessing the faith boldly in public and by adorning that confession with a worthy life, ending with a doxology.

cast.name: Lucian
cast.who: The martyr honored in this homily, who endured hunger and trial and confessed only 'I am a Christian.'

cast.name: the devil
cast.who: The enemy who tries to break Lucian through hunger, idol-food, and interrogation.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle whose words about hunger and thirst sustain Lucian.

cast.name: Noah
cast.who: Mentioned for his dove and raven, contrasting faithful return with departure.

cast.name: the three youths
cast.who: The three young men in Babylon whose table is brought to Lucian's mind as an example of faithfulness.

cast.name: the executioner
cast.who: The torturer who interrogates Lucian at his trial.

voices.speaker: Lucian (reported speech)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by verbs of saying such as ἀπεκρίνατο and φησί, with his repeated confession given in indirect speech introduced by ὅτι.

voices.speaker: the executioner (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by λέγοντος τοῦ δημίου, with his questions given in direct speech.

voices.speaker: Scripture (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as ἀκούων παρὰ τῶν θείων Γραφῶν, ὁ προφήτης ἔλεγε, and φησί, with recognizable biblical wording.

key_terms.sense: A Christian who bears witness to Christ by suffering and death; here specifically Lucian.
The martyr's contest or death, understood as a baptism in blood.
The disciplined, virtuous way of life that enables endurance of suffering.
Bold, open speech in confessing the faith before rulers and opponents.
The public confession of Christian faith, especially 'I am a Christian.'
The title Lucian uses as his complete answer, summing up his identity, homeland, family, and occupation.
Hunger used by the devil as the most severe and prolonged form of torture against Lucian.
Food sacrificed to idols, placed before Lucian as a temptation to break his fast and his faith.
A table, used both for the defiled table of idol-food and for the holy table of the Lord, which Lucian remembers.
The heavenly Jerusalem, the true homeland of Christians.
Citizenship or commonwealth, said to be in heaven for Christians.
The ark, an image for the church as a place of safety amid the storm of worldly passions.
Almsgiving, presented as a lasting treasure that cannot be stolen, unlike worldly wealth.
The contest or struggle of the martyr, an athletic image for enduring torture.

scripture: The author quotes the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and the New Testament. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint; modern citations should use the corresponding Hebrew/English Psalm numbers where they differ. Biblical books should be cited by their modern English names, with the Septuagint form noted where relevant.
uncertain: The precise date of the homily within Chrysostom's career is not established from the text.
The identity of the martyr Lucian is not specified beyond his name and the manner of his contest; the homily does not indicate which Lucian is meant.

_unresolved_facts.claim: honors the martyr Lucian, whose martyrdom he presents as a baptism in blood on this day
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Χθὲς μὲν οὖν ὁ Δεσπότης ἡμῶν ὕδατι ἐβαπτίσατο, σήμερον δὲ ὁ δοῦλος αἵματι βαπτίζεται
_unresolved_facts.fix: Chrysostom presents the martyr's blood as a baptism, but the text does not explicitly state this is Lucian's actual martyrdom day; the homily is delivered 'today' but the temporal relationship to Lucian's feast is not specified as his martyrdom anniversary

_unresolved_facts.claim: He then turns to the martyr Lucian, describing how the devil first tried to break him by prolonged hunger, and when that failed, added the further trial of placing idol-food before his eyes
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὡς δὲ εἶδεν ὁ μιαρὸς δαίμων οὐκ ἐνδιδόντα τῇ τοσαύτῃ τοῦ πράγματος ἀνάγκῃ, ἔτι χαλεπωτέραν ἐποίει τὴν βάσανον. Καὶ γὰρ εἰδωλόθυτα λαβὼν...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The devil first tried hunger, then when that failed added the trial of idol-food; but the text does not say Lucian was actually broken by either—he endured both

_unresolved_facts.claim: At his trial Lucian answered every question only with 'I am a Christian,' showing that this one confession contains his homeland, citizenship, family, and occupation
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ δὲ πρὸς ἑκάστην πεῦσιν ἀπεκρίνατο, ὅτι Χριστιανός εἰμι, μόνον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Lucian answered each question with 'I am a Christian' only; Chrysostom interprets this as containing homeland, citizenship, family, and occupation, but the text says 'only' (μόνον), and the interpretation is Chrysostom's theological expansion, not Lucian's explicit statement

_unresolved_facts.claim: the executioner (quoted)... his questions given in direct speech
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ λέγοντος τοῦ δημίου· Ποίας εἶ πατρίδος; Χριστιανός εἰμι, φησί· Τί ἔχεις ἐπιτήδευμα; Χριστιανός εἰμι· Τίνας προγόνους;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The δήμιος is not the executioner but the torturer/gaoler; and the questions are in direct speech but Lucian's replies are also in direct speech (φησί), not indirect as claimed in voices

_unresolved_facts.claim: Lucian (reported speech)... his repeated confession given in indirect speech introduced by ὅτι
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ δὲ πρὸς ἑκάστην πεῦσιν ἀπεκρίνατο, ὅτι Χριστιανός εἰμι, μόνον... καὶ λέγοντος τοῦ δημίου· Ποίας εἶ πατρίδος; Χριστιανός εἰμι, φησί
_unresolved_facts.fix: Lucian's confession is in direct speech, not indirect; the ὅτι introduces direct discourse (declarative), and φησί confirms direct speech throughout the exchange

_unresolved_facts.claim: the executioner (quoted)... his questions given in direct speech
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ λέγοντος τοῦ δημίου· Ποίας εἶ πατρίδος;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The δήμιος is the torturer/gaoler, not executioner; and while the questions are direct speech, this is not a 'voice' in the same sense—the brief misidentifies the role

_unresolved_facts.claim: the three youths... whose table is brought to Lucian's mind as an example of faithfulness
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀνεμνήσθη καὶ τῆς τραπέζης ἐκείνης τῶν τριῶν παίδων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says 'he remembered' (Ἀνεμνήσθη), but does not specify this was brought to Lucian's mind during his trial; the subject is ambiguous and could be Chrysostom's narration rather than Lucian's recollection
